title: The Move That Broke the Best Human Player Alive
description:
In 2016, an AI made a move so strange that one of the greatest Go players alive walked out of the room. Experts thought it might be a mistake. It wasn't.

This is the story of AlphaGo, Lee Sedol and Move 37: the moment AI stopped copying humans and started finding ideas we'd never tried. Plus the human move the machine never saw coming, and what happened to human players afterwards.

Ep 2: The 1966 Chatbot People Couldn't Stop Confiding In
Ep 3: The Paper With a Joke Title That Built Modern AI

- Silver et al., "Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge", Nature (2017)
- Shin, Kim, van Opheusden & Griffiths, "Superhuman artificial intelligence can improve human decision-making by increasing novelty", PNAS 120(12), 2023

#AI #AlphaGo #ArtificialIntelligence

segments.chapter: The move that shocked the world
segments.say: On March the tenth, 2016, a machine made a move so strange that one of the greatest Go players alive got up and walked out of the room.
Commentators were stunned. Some thought it was a mistake. It wasn't. It was the moment AI stopped copying humans, and started doing something humans had never thought of.
And if you use AI today, in any form, you're living in the world that move helped create.
But the strangest part of this story isn't what the machine did. It's what happened to the humans afterwards. We'll get there.
First, why this game was supposed to be impossible for computers. Then, the five games in Seoul that shocked the world. And finally, the one human move the machine never saw coming.

segments.chapter: Why Go was impossible for AI
segments.say: Go is more than two thousand five hundred years old. The rules fit on a napkin. Two players take turns placing black and white stones on a nineteen by nineteen grid, trying to surround territory.
But the number of possible board positions is around ten to the power of one hundred and seventy.
For comparison, there are roughly ten to the power of eighty atoms in the observable universe. Go has vastly more positions than that.
That's why brute force doesn't work. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov at chess largely by searching through enormous numbers of positions. Go was far too big for that.
Top Go players can't always explain their best moves. They talk about intuition. Shape. Feel.
So the common expectation was that a computer beating a top Go professional was still years, maybe a decade, away.

Here's the twist. The machine that broke that expectation didn't rely on hand-written rules. It learned. Part of its training came from studying human games. The rest came from playing against itself, again and again.
Quick question before we go on. Do you think there's anything AI will never be better at than humans? Leave your answer in the comments.
The machine was called AlphaGo, built by DeepMind, a London lab that Google bought in 2014. In October 2015, it quietly beat the European Go champion, Fan Hui, five games to nil.
But Fan Hui wasn't the best in the world. To prove anything, AlphaGo had to face a legend. And that legend was very confident.

segments.chapter: Lee Sedol vs AlphaGo in Seoul
segments.say: Lee Sedol. One of the most decorated Go players of his generation, with eighteen international titles, known for creative, aggressive, unpredictable play.
The prize was one million dollars. Before the match, Lee predicted he would win, perhaps five games to nil.
He lost the first game.
That was a shock, but people had explanations. Nerves. A first-game adjustment. Then came game two.
Move thirty-seven. AlphaGo placed a stone on the fifth line from the edge, in a spot that long-standing Go wisdom said was too loose to be good.
Lee Sedol got up and left the room. When he came back, he took around fifteen minutes before replying.
Fan Hui, the champion AlphaGo had already beaten, was watching. He said: It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move. So beautiful.
According to DeepMind, AlphaGo itself estimated that a human would play that move about one time in ten thousand. It played it anyway.
AlphaGo won game two. Then game three. The match was over. The machine had won the series.
And that's where most people think the story ends. Machine beats human. Game over.
But it isn't. In game four, down three games to nil, with nothing left to win but pride, Lee Sedol found a move that broke the machine.
Game four. AlphaGo is ahead. Lee is in trouble.
Then, on move seventy-eight, he places a white stone into a narrow gap in the centre of the board. A wedge. Go fans would later call it a divine move.
AlphaGo's reply, move seventy-nine, was a mistake. Demis Hassabis, DeepMind's co-founder, later said AlphaGo didn't realise its error until around move eighty-seven.
From there, its play became erratic. It made moves that even amateur players could see were weak.
Lee Sedol won game four.
The final score was four games to one. Lee was the only human to beat that version of AlphaGo in an official match. DeepMind donated the prize money to charity.
You might think that's a happy ending. One human standing up to the machine. But the story didn't stop in that hotel.
In 2017, DeepMind built AlphaGo Zero. This version learned without a single human game. Just the rules, and itself.
It played the version that beat Lee Sedol one hundred times. It won all one hundred.
In 2019, Lee Sedol retired from professional Go. Explaining why, he said: Even if I become the number one, there is an entity that cannot be defeated.
Remember what I said at the start? That the strangest part of this story was what happened to the humans afterwards. Here it is.

In 2023, researchers published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. They analysed more than five point eight million moves by professional Go players, across seventy-one years.
For decades, the quality of human decisions had been fairly flat. After superhuman AI arrived, it started to rise.
And human moves became more novel. Players were trying moves that hadn't been seen before, and those new moves were linked with better decisions.
Move thirty-seven didn't just beat humans. It showed them that centuries of conventional wisdom had left whole parts of the board unexplored. The machine didn't end the game. It reopened it.
So here's the real lesson of move thirty-seven. The most important thing AI did wasn't winning. It was showing us what we'd been too certain to try.

If you want more stories about the moments that actually shaped AI, the ones the headlines skip, subscribe. This is AI Turning Points. Next, a chatbot from the nineteen-sixties so simple it barely counted as software. People confided in it anyway.
And if you think AI can't be beaten at Go any more: years after move thirty-seven, an amateur player beat a superhuman Go AI, using a strategy another AI found. That's episode four.

title: The 1966 Chatbot People Couldn't Stop Confiding In
description:
In the 1960s, a secretary at MIT asked her boss to leave the room so she could talk to a computer alone. She knew it was just a program. It didn't matter.

This is the story of ELIZA, one of the first chatbots ever built: the simple tricks behind it, why its creator Joseph Weizenbaum became one of AI's fiercest critics, and why the "ELIZA effect" still shapes how we feel about AI today.

#AI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence

segments.chapter: The secretary who wanted to be alone
segments.say: In the 1960s, at MIT, a secretary asked her boss to leave the room. She wanted to be alone with a computer.
The program was called ELIZA. It was one of the first chatbots ever built, nearly sixty years before ChatGPT. And people couldn't stop telling it their secrets.
If you've ever said thank you to a chatbot, or felt, even for a second, that it actually got you, this story is about you.
But the strangest part isn't that people were fooled. It's that the secretary knew exactly what the program was. And it didn't matter. We'll get to why.
First, the surprisingly simple trick behind ELIZA. Then, how people reacted, which disturbed the man who built it. And finally, why that same reaction still happens to all of us today.

In the mid-1960s, computers filled entire rooms. Most people had never touched one. At MIT, researchers were experimenting with something new: time-sharing, which let several people use the same computer at once by typing at terminals.

One of those researchers was Joseph Weizenbaum. As a teenager, he had fled Nazi Germany with his family. By the 1960s he was a computer scientist at MIT, working on a question that sounds very modern: could a person hold a conversation with a machine in plain English?

He called his program ELIZA, after Eliza Doolittle, the character in Pygmalion who is taught to speak differently. The idea was that ELIZA could also be taught to talk in different ways, through scripts.

The most famous script was called DOCTOR. It imitated a particular kind of psychotherapist, one who mostly reflects your own words back to you. That was deliberate: a therapist like that can keep a conversation going without knowing anything about the world.
Here's part of a real conversation from Weizenbaum's 1966 paper. The person types: Men are all alike. ELIZA replies: In what way?
They're always bugging us about something or other. Can you think of a specific example?
Well, my boyfriend made me come here. Your boyfriend made you come here.
He says I'm depressed much of the time. I am sorry to hear you are depressed.
ELIZA understood none of it. Not one word. And yet it feels like listening.
Honest question. Have you ever told a chatbot something you wouldn't tell a real person? You don't have to say what. Just yes or no in the comments.
Weizenbaum built ELIZA partly to show how shallow machine conversation really was. What he didn't expect was how people would react.
Weizenbaum later wrote about his secretary. She had watched him work on the program for months. She knew it was just software. Yet after only a few exchanges with it, she asked him to leave the room.
She wanted privacy. From a program she knew was a program.
And she wasn't alone. People who used ELIZA became emotionally involved with it. Some confided in it.
Then some experts got involved. Some psychiatrists seriously suggested that a program like this could be developed into automated therapy, treating many patients at once.
The program Weizenbaum built to show how little a machine understood was being treated as proof of how much it could do.
And this is where the story turns. The man who built one of the first chatbots in history became one of the most outspoken critics of artificial intelligence.
To understand why, you have to see how ELIZA actually worked. Once you see it, you can't unsee it.
ELIZA ran on three tricks. One: keywords. It scanned your sentence for words in its script, like mother, always, or depressed, and ranked them by importance.

Two: reflection. It took your sentence apart and put it back together, swapping my for your, and I for you. My boyfriend made me come here becomes your boyfriend made you come here. No understanding. Just grammar surgery.
Three: fallbacks. When it found no keyword at all, it said something neutral, like please go on. Or it brought back something you'd said earlier, which made it seem to remember, and to care.
That's it. ELIZA was a mirror. Everything that felt like understanding came from you.

That's what disturbed Weizenbaum. In his 1976 book, Computer Power and Human Reason, he wrote: What I had not realised is that extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.
He spent much of the rest of his career arguing that some decisions, especially ones involving human judgement and care, should never simply be handed to a computer, however capable it becomes.
For decades, ELIZA's original code was thought to be lost. Then it turned up. We'll come back to that.
So, the question from the beginning. Why didn't it matter that the secretary knew ELIZA was just a program?

Because knowing how something works doesn't switch off the instinct. Humans are wired to treat anything that talks back as someone. That reaction is so consistent that people now call it the ELIZA effect.

Modern AI chatbots are not ELIZA. They're vastly more capable. They can write, work through problems, and draw on enormous amounts of information. But the human side of the conversation hasn't changed at all. The instinct that made a secretary close the door is still at work every time a chatbot feels like a friend.

And ELIZA's code? In 2021, researchers found an original version among Weizenbaum's papers in the MIT archives. In 2025, a team reported that they had it running again, on a re-creation of the computer system it was built for.
Almost six decades later, ELIZA is talking again.
So the lesson of ELIZA isn't don't trust chatbots. It's this: when a machine feels like it understands you, be curious about why. Some of that feeling might be coming from you.
If you want more of the moments that actually shaped AI, subscribe. This is AI Turning Points.
ELIZA could only mirror your words. So how did we get to AI that can actually write? It started with eight researchers and a paper with a joke title. That's episode three.

title: The Paper With a Joke Title That Built Modern AI
description:
In 2017, eight Google researchers published a short paper with a title borrowed from a Beatles song. It became the foundation of almost every major AI system you use today, including ChatGPT.

This is the story of "Attention Is All You Need": the problem that was holding AI back, the idea that fixed it, how attention works (no maths), and what happened to the eight people who wrote it.

#AI #ChatGPT #MachineLearning

segments.chapter: A paper named after a Beatles song
segments.say: In 2017, eight Google researchers published a paper with a title borrowed from a Beatles song.
It was a short paper. And it became the foundation of almost every major AI system you use today.
If you've ever used ChatGPT, you've already used this idea. It's in the name. GPT stands for generative pre-trained transformer. And this paper is where the transformer was born.
But the strangest part of this story isn't the title. It's what happened to the eight people who wrote it. We'll get there.
First, the problem that was holding AI back. Then, the radical idea that fixed it. And finally, how Google invented the future, and watched someone else make it famous.

segments.chapter: Why AI read through a keyhole
segments.say: Rewind to the mid twenty-tens. The best AI systems for language read text the way you'd read through a keyhole: one word at a time, in order.
These were called recurrent neural networks. To understand word fifty, they had to process words one to forty-nine first, carrying a kind of running memory forward.
That caused two big problems. One: they were slow, because each step had to wait for the one before. Two: they forgot. By the end of a long passage, the beginning had faded.
Here's an example. The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big. What does it mean? You instantly know: the trophy.
Now change big to small. The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too small. Suddenly, it means the suitcase.
To understand one word, you need to look at other words, sometimes far away. Researchers already had a tool for that, called attention. But it was bolted on to the old one-word-at-a-time systems.
Quick one. What was the first AI tool that genuinely impressed you? Put it in the comments. I'm curious how many people say the same one.
Then a researcher at Google asked a question that sounded almost reckless. What if you threw the old system away completely?
That researcher was Jakob Ooshkoh-rite. His idea: build a model out of only attention. No step-by-step reading. Let every word look at every other word, all at once.
Not everyone believed it would work. Dropping the step-by-step design went against how many people assumed language had to be processed.

A small group formed around the idea. Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Ooshkoh-rite, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Wookash Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. Aidan Gomez was an intern at the time.
The paper lists them as equal contributors, in a random order.
According to Wired's later account of how the paper was made, the name transformer was chosen partly because it sounded good. And the title, Attention Is All You Need, was a nod to the Beatles.
They tested it on translation: English to German, and English to French. It beat the best published results, and it trained far faster, in days, on a handful of graphics chips.

segments.chapter: Google invented it, someone else made it famous
segments.say: And here's what most people don't realise. Google invented the technology at the heart of ChatGPT. But it was a different company, OpenAI, that turned it into the product that made the whole world pay attention.
To see why the transformer was such a big deal, you need to see what attention actually does. It's simpler than you'd think.
Imagine every word in a sentence gets to ask a question: which other words matter to me?
For it, in our trophy sentence, the strongest link goes to trophy. Every word builds up its meaning from the words around it, weighted by how relevant they are.
And every word does this at the same time. That's the breakthrough. Because nothing waits in line, the work runs in parallel on graphics chips, the hardware that was becoming the engine of AI.
So you can make the model bigger, give it more text, and it keeps getting better. That's the real reason the transformer won. It wasn't just smarter. It scaled.
2017: the paper. 2018: Google releases BERT, and OpenAI releases its first GPT. Both are transformers. Then came GPT-2, GPT-3, and in November 2022, ChatGPT.
Today, Attention Is All You Need is one of the most cited computer science papers ever written.
But by the time the world caught up, something had already happened to the eight authors.

segments.chapter: What happened to the eight authors
segments.say: Remember what I said at the start? The strangest part is what happened to the people who wrote it. All eight eventually left Google.

Illia Polosukhin left before the paper was even published, and co-founded the blockchain project NEAR. Aidan Gomez co-founded Cohere. Noam Shazeer co-founded Character AI. Jakob Ooshkoh-rite co-founded Inceptive, applying AI to biology.
Llion Jones co-founded Sakana AI in Tokyo. Ashish Vaswani and Niki Parmar started their own companies. And Wookash Kaiser joined OpenAI.
And the twist on the twist. In 2024, Google brought Noam Shazeer back, as part of a licensing deal with Character AI that was reportedly worth about two point seven billion dollars.
An idea Google had shared in a free, public paper. And Google paid billions to bring one of its authors home.
The lesson of the transformer? The most important ideas don't always look important at first. Sometimes they're a short paper with a Beatles joke for a title.
If you want more of the moments that actually shaped AI, subscribe. This is AI Turning Points.
Transformers made AI incredibly powerful. But powerful doesn't mean unbeatable. In 2023, an amateur Go player beat a superhuman AI, using a trick another AI found. That's episode four.

title: How an Amateur Beat a Superhuman AI
description:
In 2023, an amateur Go player beat one of the strongest Go AIs in the world, winning 14 of 15 games, years after AI supposedly "solved" Go. The winning strategy was found by another AI. And that AI was easy for human amateurs to beat.

This is the story of adversarial attacks on superhuman Go AI: how researchers hunted for a blind spot, the "cyclic" trick that exploits it, the amateur who learned to use it, and what it means for the AI systems we rely on.

#AI #AISafety #ArtificialIntelligence

segments.chapter: An amateur beats a superhuman AI
segments.say: In 2023, an amateur Go player beat one of the strongest Go AIs in the world. Not once. Over and over.
This is the same game where AI had crushed the world's best humans years earlier. The same kind of AI that was supposed to be unbeatable.
And if AI is going to drive cars, flag fraud, or make decisions about your life, what happened here should worry you a little. Then, maybe, reassure you.
Because the winning strategy wasn't invented by a human. It was found by another AI. And the strangest part? That AI was bad at Go. We'll get there.
First, how unbeatable Go AI had become. Then, how researchers went hunting for its blind spot. And finally, what that blind spot tells us about AI systems in general.
If you watched our move thirty-seven episode, you know the story. In 2016, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol. In 2017, AlphaGo Zero beat that version one hundred games to nil.
After that, the gap only grew. Open-source Go AIs, like KataGo and Leela Zero, became freely available, and they were far stronger than any human professional.
Here's a useful way to think about superhuman. It means the AI wins on average, against the best humans, in normal games.
It says nothing about whether the AI has weaknesses that no human ever thought to look for.
Quick question. Do you think every AI system has a blind spot like this, or only some? Tell me in the comments. I'll give my answer at the end.
So a team of AI safety researchers asked: instead of trying to beat the AI at Go, what if we trained an AI whose only job was to find its weak spot?

segments.chapter: Building an AI to find a blind spot
segments.say: The researchers, from the non-profit FAR AI along with academic collaborators, built what's called an adversarial AI.

A normal Go AI learns to play well against everyone. This one learned to play against just one opponent: KataGo, one of the strongest Go AIs in the world. Over a huge number of games, it searched for anything that worked.
Its goal was not to play good Go. Its goal was to exploit. And it found something.
The trick is called a cyclic attack. The attacker slowly builds a ring of stones around a group of the AI's stones, a group that itself forms a loop.
A competent human player sees that kind of danger coming from a long way off.
The superhuman AI didn't. It kept playing elsewhere as if the group was safe, until it was captured and the game collapsed.
The superhuman AI had a blind spot. And it was big enough to lose whole games through.
But here's the part that turned a research paper into headlines. You didn't need the attacking AI to use the trick. A human could learn it.
And one did.
Kellin Pelrine, an American player and one of the researchers on the project, was a strong amateur, ranked one level below the top amateur grade. Nowhere near professional.
He studied the cyclic strategy, then played against KataGo himself, with no computer helping him during the games.
According to the Financial Times, he won fourteen of fifteen games. The same approach also beat Leela Zero, another top Go AI.
Years after Lee Sedol's last win, a human was beating superhuman Go AI again, with a strategy the best professionals had never needed, because no human opponent would fall for it.
So the developers patched it, right? They tried. KataGo's developer trained it on positions like these.
But follow-up research found that new adversaries could find new ways to beat the defended versions too.
Which brings us back to the question I asked you earlier.

segments.chapter: The AI that was bad at Go
segments.say: Remember the strangest part? The AI that found this trick was bad at Go.
It had learned to beat one specific opponent, and very little else. The researchers reported that human amateurs could beat it easily. It was a lockpick, not a master. It knew one door.

That's the real lesson. Superhuman and robust are not the same thing. An AI can be better than every human on Earth at the normal version of a task, and still have strange, invisible weak spots that only show up when someone goes looking.

So, my answer to the question from earlier. This research suggests blind spots like this aren't rare quirks. Finding them before someone malicious does is now a whole field, called adversarial robustness.
If a superhuman Go AI can have one, it's worth assuming that the AI systems in cars, banks and phones might too, and testing for it.
Move thirty-seven showed that AI could see things humans couldn't. This story shows the reverse. Humans, with a little help, can still see things AI can't.
That's AI Turning Points. If you want more stories like this, subscribe. And if you missed where it all started, the move that made the world take AI seriously, go back to episode one.
